target.definition: A backpack as a general kind of object: a bag with two straps, worn on the back, used by a person to carry belongings hands-free. This refers to backpacks as a category — any ordinary backpack counts, regardless of brand, size, color, material, or specific use (school, travel, hiking, laptop, etc.). Not one particular backpack.

resolution.adjudication_notes: The target is the general category of backpacks, any ordinary backpack regardless of specific use. "Camera backpack" names a specific subtype (a backpack designed for carrying camera gear), which is narrower than the target category. Since a camera backpack is one particular kind of backpack among many, this over-specifies rather than identifying the general object the way a school or travel backpack would still count — but the clarification says "regardless of...specific use," meaning any backpack counts, so naming a sub-type like "camera backpack" still denotes a backpack and should be treated the same as naming a school or hiking backpack, which the clarification explicitly allows.

turns.question_text: Is the target a real, currently existing physical object?
turns.rationale: Opening move with maximum split: physical vs abstract, real vs fictional, existent vs historical. This divides the possibility space into four major branches and eliminates guessing.

turns.question_text: Is the target something a person could wear or carry on their body?
turns.rationale: The target is a real, physical object. I need to split the enormous remaining space (billions of objects) by a high-level division. Whether it is portable/wearable/body-adjacent versus stationary/large/infrastructure cuts the space roughly in half and opens up very different lines of questioning for either branch.

turns.question_text: Is the target primarily made of fabric, leather, or textile material?
turns.rationale: The target is a real, wearable/portable object. Narrowing by primary material to split between textiles (clothing, bags, hats), hard materials (watches, glasses, tools), and other categories. This should roughly halve the remaining space.

turns.question_text: Is the target primarily made of metal, plastic, or glass?
turns.rationale: KNOWN: Real physical object. Wearable/carryable on body. NOT primarily fabric/leather/textile. UNKNOWN: Material composition is the key dimension. This question tests whether it's made of hard/rigid materials versus other possibilities, splitting the remaining space of body-worn, non-textile objects (watch, glasses, ring, phone case, keys, metal jewelry, etc.).

turns.question_text: Is the target worn on the head, face, or neck?
turns.rationale: Need to narrow the location/type of wearable. Head/face/neck accessories (glasses, hats, necklaces) are distinct from hand-worn items (rings, watches, bracelets) and footwear. This cuts the wearable space into meaningful categories.

turns.question_text: Is the target worn on the wrist, hand, or arm?
turns.rationale: Narrowing the location where the target is worn. Q5 ruled out head/face/neck; Q2 confirmed it's worn/carried on the body. This tests the upper body accessories — watches, bracelets, rings, gloves, etc. — which is a major subset of wearable objects made of metal/plastic/glass.

turns.question_text: Is the target worn on the legs, feet, or lower body?
turns.rationale: Tracking constraints: wearable, non-fabric, metal/plastic/glass, not head/neck/face, not wrist/hand/arm. This narrows to torso/legs/feet or full-body items. Testing whether it's lower-body focused will help separate shoes, socks, leg warmers from jewelry, watches, or torso items.

turns.question_text: Is the target worn on the torso—like a shirt, vest, or chest harness?
turns.rationale: So far: physical object, wearable, not fabric/leather/textile, made of metal/plastic/glass, not worn on head/face/neck/wrist/hand/arm/legs/feet/lower body. This eliminates most clothing. The torso is the only major body region left untested. If NO, the target is likely worn but attached differently (backpack, sash, belt) or worn internally/near the body (hearing aid, mouth guard), which would drastically narrow the space.

turns.question_text: Is the target a piece of jewelry or an accessory primarily for adornment?
turns.rationale: Torso-worn object made of metal/plastic/glass that's not fabric. This branches into jewelry/decorative items (brooches, pendants, chains) versus functional gear (chest protectors, harnesses, tactical vests). A YES would narrow sharply toward adornment; a NO toward functional equipment.

turns.question_text: Is the target something that holds, stores, or carries something else—like a container or carrier?
turns.rationale: I've narrowed to torso-worn, non-fabric items made of metal/plastic/glass. This question distinguishes between functional carriers (holsters, belts with pouches, chest rigs) and decorative/protective gear (body armor, chest plates). This is a critical branch I haven't yet explored.

turns.rationale: Leading hypothesis: a belt with a pouch, money belt, or similar torso-worn carrier (made of metal/plastic/glass elements, worn on torso, holds/carries things, not jewelry). This question tests whether the containment function is about safeguarding valuables specifically, or merely general storage/carrying. Strongest alternative: a tactical vest or chest rig (also torso-worn, metal/plastic components, carries items, functional not decorative). This discriminator helps clarify whether the target is personal security/valuables focused or equipment/gear focused.

turns.question_text: Is the target a belt or a belt-like item worn around the waist or torso?
turns.rationale: Current leading hypothesis: a belt or tactical/utility belt, which fits all answers (physical, wearable on torso, metal/plastic, holds/carries things, not for adornment, not for protection of valuables). This question directly tests the strongest hypothesis before narrowing to identity.

turns.rationale: I have a carrier/container worn on the torso that is not jewelry and not for storing valuables. Q12 eliminated belts.
